o: Two threads share one `FooBar` instance: thread A runs `foo()` printing "foo" n times, thread B runs `bar()` printing "bar" n times. We must interleave them so the output is exactly "foobar" repeated n times, with no reordering like "foofoo" or "barbar". For n = 1 the only valid output is "foobar"; for n = 2 it is "foobarfoobar", meaning after each "foo" a "bar" must follow before the next "foo". Since 1 <= n <= 1000, any correct synchronization mechanism is fast enough; the challenge is purely about ordering, not performance. The key requirement is mutual signaling: foo must wait until bar has finished the previous iteration (or until the start), and bar must wait for foo.
k: This is an ordering problem: enforce strict alternation foo -> bar -> foo -> bar ... using synchronization primitives.
Any pairwise signaling mechanism works: semaphores, condition variables with a flag, or atomics/spin-waiting.
The first print must be "foo", so bar must initially block while foo starts unblocked.

a.i: Use one semaphore per thread as a token-passing system. The fooSemaphore starts available so foo prints first; barSemaphore starts at zero so bar blocks. After printing "foo", foo releases bar's semaphore; after printing "bar", bar releases foo's semaphore. This creates a strict ping-pong handshake for all n iterations.
s: Create fooSemaphore initialized to 1 and barSemaphore initialized to 0.
In foo(), loop n times: acquire fooSemaphore, print "foo", release barSemaphore.
In bar(), loop n times: acquire barSemaphore, print "bar", release fooSemaphore.
a.t: O(n) time — each of the 2n prints happens once, and semaphore operations are O(1).
a.sp: O(1) extra space — just two semaphores regardless of n.

a.n: Approach 2: Condition Variable with a Turn Flag
a.i: Guard a shared boolean `fooTurn` with a mutex and condition variable. foo waits while it is not its turn, prints, sets fooTurn to false and notifies; bar does the symmetric thing. This avoids busy waiting because waiters sleep until notified, and it generalizes naturally to more complex ordering patterns.
s: Initialize fooTurn = true, plus a mutex and condition_variable.
In foo(), loop n times: lock, wait on cv while !fooTurn, print "foo", set fooTurn = false, notify_all, unlock.
In bar(), loop n times: lock, wait on cv while fooTurn, print "bar", set fooTurn = true, notify_all, unlock.
a.t: O(n) time — 2n prints plus O(1) synchronization work per iteration.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — one flag, one mutex, one condition variable.

w: In an interview, lead with the semaphore approach since it maps most directly onto the alternating-token intuition, then mention the condition-variable version if asked about alternatives or if semaphores are unavailable. Common pitfalls: forgetting that bar must block initially (otherwise "barfoo" may be printed), using notify instead of notifyAll when multiple threads could wait, busy-spinning without yielding in JavaScript, and calling wait without holding the lock. Edge cases are trivial (n = 1 still requires correct initial ordering). Likely follow-ups: generalize to k threads printing in round-robin order, extend to a pattern like "foofoobar", or discuss why spin-waiting on atomics wastes CPU compared to blocking primitives.
